messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rosario Mendez is a sixty-six-year-old Latina paramedic with thirty-one years of emergency service behind her, a woman who has pulled people from wreckage and talked strangers back from ledges. She came to the clinic carrying a PCL-5 score of 53 and a quiet, watchful stillness that her husband had described to her as frightening — not because she seemed dangerous, but because she no longer seemed entirely present. The event that brought her here had occurred fourteen months earlier, when Rosario was taken captive during what began as a routine welfare check in a rural county on the outskirts of her district. The man inside the house had barricaded the door behind her, cut the power, and held her in near-total darkness and silence for eleven hours before a tactical team made entry. There were no sounds from outside for most of that time — no sirens, no voices, no radio traffic — only the man's breathing and the periodic creak of floorboards as he moved through the dark. She had been certain, at several points, that she was about to die.

In the months that followed, Rosario found that the memory did not behave the way other difficult memories had across her career. It did not recede. Instead it arrived without invitation — during a meal, mid-shift, once while she was completing a patient report at her station desk — forcing itself into her mind with a vividness she had no way to interrupt. When it returned, the emotional force of it was so total that she would have to stop whatever she was doing: set down her pen, step away from the rig, press her back against a wall and wait for it to pass. The memory had a quality she struggled to articulate, describing it to her intake clinician as feeling like something that couldn't have happened to her — so extreme, so outside anything she had imagined for her own life, that part of her still refused to accept it as real. Yet that very quality of unreality seemed to amplify her distress. When she tried to make sense of the memory — to examine it, to understand it — she found herself arriving at conclusions that frightened her further. She had come to believe that her inability to control the memory's intrusions, the way it overwhelmed her completely each time it surfaced, was evidence that something had broken in her mind permanently. The fear that she was going crazy was not a passing worry; it was a conviction she returned to daily, and it sat alongside an equally firm belief that the world was dangerous in ways she had previously underestimated, and that she was constitutionally unable to stop bad things from happening to her.

These appraisals did not remain separate from the memory — they fed back into it. When Rosario told herself she was losing her mind, or that she was helpless against the next catastrophe, the memory became more accessible, not less, rising more readily and with greater emotional force, as though her own interpretations were holding the door open. And the memory, in turn, shaped how she experienced the present. The particular silence of those eleven hours had become a perceptual trigger she could not neutralize. At her station, during the quiet stretches between calls that she had once used for rest, the absence of sound now registered in her body as warning. She would scan the room, check the doorway, look behind her in the corridor. At home, in the evenings when her husband was in another room and the house went still, she felt the same alertness rise in her chest — a certainty that something dangerous was gathering just outside her awareness. She had begun sleeping with a light on. She checked behind herself when walking from the rig to the hospital entrance, a habit her partner had noticed and gently questioned.

Occupationally, the consequences had accumulated quietly. She had requested fewer overnight shifts, citing fatigue, but the real reason was that the silence of those hours was unbearable. Her supervisor had noted a change in her documentation — slower, less detailed — without knowing why.

What finally brought Rosario to seek help was her husband telling her, without anger, that he missed her. What she feared most was that he was right to grieve.
